summary.text: An acid–base reaction is a chemical reaction that happens between an acid and a base.
In the Brønsted–Lowry view, an acid–base reaction removes a proton from the acid and adds it to the base.
Several theories define acids and bases, and they complement each other: Lewis is the broadest and Arrhenius the most restrictive.

facts.label: Conjugate base
facts.value: The acid with a proton removed

facts.label: Arrhenius acid
facts.value: Ionises in water to form hydrogen cations

facts.value: Only applies to substances in water

facts.value: Formulated in 1923 by Brønsted and Lowry

items.prompt: A base takes a proton from an acid in a reaction. What has the base turned into?

options.label: A salt that can no longer react
A stronger base with a larger charge
Its conjugate acid, the base with a proton added
The solvent that the proton was dissolved in

items.explain: Receiving a proton gives the base its conjugate acid, which is the base with a proton added.

items.prompt: A chemist uses Arrhenius's idea to decide whether a dissolved substance is a base. What must it do to count?

options.label: Raise the concentration of hydrogen ions in the solution
Raise the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution
Accept a proton handed over by another molecule
Accept an electron pair to form a new bond

items.explain: An Arrhenius base increases hydroxide ions in an aqueous solution. Raising hydrogen ions defines an Arrhenius acid.

items.prompt: Pure HCl dissolved in toluene is not acidic by Arrhenius's definition. What limit of that definition explains this?

options.label: It only covers acids that contain a metal atom
It only covers reactions that give off heat
It only covers acids that have no hydrogen in them
It only covers substances that are dissolved in water

items.explain: Arrhenius's definition is restricted to aqueous solutions, so it fails for non-aqueous cases like HCl in toluene. That led to the Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis theories.

items.prompt: In a reaction, one molecule hands a hydrogen cation to a second molecule. In the Brønsted–Lowry view, what is the first molecule?

options.label: The acid, because it donates the proton
The base, because it donates the proton
The salt, because it carries the proton
The solvent, because it holds the proton

items.explain: Brønsted–Lowry acids donate hydrogen cations (protons) and bases accept them.

items.prompt: A student says the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis theories contradict each other, so only one can be right. What is the better view?

options.label: Arrhenius is the correct one and the later ones are mistakes
Lewis is the narrowest, so the others replaced it
They complement each other, from Lewis as broadest to Arrhenius as narrowest
They apply in different centuries and are now all retired

items.explain: The models complement each other. Lewis has the broadest definition, Brønsted–Lowry is a subset of it, and Arrhenius is the most restrictive.

items.prompt: A cake batter rises in the oven after baking powder meets water. What makes the bubbles?

options.label: Baking soda and acidic salts react and release carbon dioxide gas
Baking soda alone boils away as steam in the heat
The acidic salts burn off as a cloud of smoke
The liquid splits apart into hydrogen and oxygen gas

items.explain: Baking powder is baking soda plus acidic salts. With water, they react to give gaseous carbon dioxide, which forms the bubbles.

beats.prompt: Match each Arrhenius or Brønsted–Lowry term to what it does.
beats.explain: Arrhenius defined acids and bases by the ions they form in water. Brønsted–Lowry defined them by whether they donate or accept protons.

beats.prompt: Put these ideas about acids and bases in the order they were proposed.
beats.explain: Lavoisier came around 1776, Liebig in 1838, Arrhenius's work in 1884, and Brønsted and Lowry in 1923.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Arrhenius's definition only applies to substances dissolved in water.
So pure HCl dissolved in toluene is not acidic by his definition.
So HCl in toluene must be a base.

beats.explain: Falling outside the Arrhenius definition does not make it a base. The definition simply does not apply, which pushed chemists toward the Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis theories.

paragraphs.heading: Acid meets base
paragraphs.text: An acid–base reaction is a reaction between an acid and a base. One practical use is titration, which can be used to find pH. Chemists have several theories of what acids and bases are, and these are best seen as fitting together rather than competing. The Lewis model has the broadest definition, the Brønsted–Lowry theory covers a subset of it, and the Arrhenius theory is the narrowest.

paragraphs.heading: Early ideas
paragraphs.text: In 1754 Guillaume-François Rouelle first proposed the idea of an acid–base reaction. He brought the word "base" into chemistry for something that turns an acid solid by reacting with it, forming a salt. Antoine Lavoisier gave the first scientific concept of acids and bases around 1776. Jöns Jacob Berzelius later described acids as oxides of nonmetals and bases as oxides of metals. In 1838 Justus von Liebig said instead that an acid contains hydrogen that a metal can replace, and his definition stayed in use for almost 50 years.

paragraphs.heading: Arrhenius and ions
paragraphs.text: Svante Arrhenius gave the first modern definition in molecular terms. It grew out of his 1884 work with Friedrich Wilhelm Ostwald showing that ions are present in water solutions, and it led to his 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. An Arrhenius acid raises the concentration of hydrogen ions, H⁺, in water, and an Arrhenius base raises the concentration of hydroxide ions, OH⁻. A bare proton does not exist freely in water; the acid protonates water, making the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺. That is why H⁺ is now read as shorthand for H₃O⁺.

paragraphs.heading: Where Arrhenius falls short
paragraphs.text: The Arrhenius definitions only hold in water and fail for most other solvents. By that rule, pure H₂SO₄ and HCl dissolved in toluene would not count as acidic, and molten NaOH would not count as alkaline. These gaps led to the Brønsted–Lowry theory and, after it, the Lewis theory.

paragraphs.heading: Passing protons
paragraphs.text: In 1923 Johannes Brønsted in Denmark and Martin Lowry in England, working independently, described acids as substances that hand over hydrogen ions, also called protons, to bases, which take them. An acid–base reaction is then a proton leaving the acid and joining the base. What is left of the acid after it loses its proton is its conjugate base. The base with its new proton is its conjugate acid. So the reaction makes not a salt and a solvent but a new acid and a new base.

paragraphs.heading: In the kitchen
paragraphs.text: Baking powder puts this chemistry to work. It is a mix of baking soda, which is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), and acidic salts. Once water is added, the bicarbonate and the acid salts react and give off carbon dioxide gas. Millions of tiny bubbles of it make the dough for bread and cakes rise.
